newsitem.title: USA: Albright lobbies on China rights resolution.
newsitem.headline: Albright lobbies on China rights resolution.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has telephoned the German, Spanish and Australian foreign ministers in an effort to prevent China from blocking debate on a U.N. human rights resolution, the State Department said on Monday.

The resolution is due to come up for a vote on Tuesday at the U.N. Human Rights Comission in Geneva. China was expected to try to prevent debate on its controversial human rights record by seeking approval of a motion of "no action."

"We really would hope that a no-action motion would not succeed because that would deny the United Nations the forum for which it was created -- the U.N. Human Rights Commission," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

"And that is to discuss difficult issues pertaining to human rights of a very large segment of the world's population. That's an important issue for us. And that's why she (Albright) made these phone calls to the Australian, German and Spanish governments over the weekend."
Burns did not say if she felt she had succeeded in winning support from any of the three. Germany and Spain are NATO allies and Australia is a close friend of the United States.

Although U.S. officials privately expressed confidence they would get good support, diplomats said a Chinese motion for "no action" on the resolution was likely to be passed as easily as it was last year.

As current holder of the European Union's rotating presidency, the Netherlands was originally due to be the resolution's main sponsor on behalf of the whole Union. But it refused to go ahead when France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Greece said they could not support it.

The United States, as it has done almost daily for a week, reaffirmed on Monday that it would give full backing to the resolution calling on China to observe human rights and protect the ethnic identity of Tibetans.

Burns said the United States believes "that as the world's premier multilateral human rights forum, the Human Rights Commission is a particularly appropriate venue" for discussing China's rights record.

"And we hope very much that the other countries that are members of the U.N. Human Rights Commission will take a stand in favour of the universality of human rights principles, and that they will vote with Denmark and the United States and other countries to bring the issue to the floor for a formal discussion and for a vote," he said.
